text: The emperor (literally: "the biggest person") loved clothes. He had lots of them, but he always wanted new ones (literally: "ones seen for the first time"). Two swindlers came and said: "We can make the most beautiful clothes." "Foolish people (literally: 'people whose heads aren't good') can't see these clothes." The emperor gave them lots of money. They took it, but didn't make anything at all. The emperor came to look. He couldn't see anything! But he was afraid: "If I say I can't see them, people will say I'm a fool." So he said: "How beautiful!" The emperor "put on" the clothes and went out. People on the street all said: "How beautiful!" They were afraid too. Then a little boy said: "He has no clothes on!" Everyone laughed: "It's true, he has no clothes!" The emperor knew they were right, but he kept on walking.

blind.whole: A man, called 'the biggest person', loves clothes and wants clothes nobody has seen before. Two people come and lie to him. They say they can make the most beautiful clothes, and that people who are not clever cannot see them. He pays them a lot of money. They take it and make nothing. When he comes to look he sees nothing, but he is afraid that if he says so, people will think he is not clever. So he calls the clothes beautiful and puts on the clothes that do not exist. He goes out. The people on the road also say the clothes are beautiful, because they are afraid too. Then a little boy says the man has no clothes on. Everyone laughs and agrees. The man knows they are right, but he keeps on walking.
blind.unsure: 'Zui da-de ren', literally 'the biggest person', appears all through the text. I read it as the most important person, the one at the top, like a ruler. It could also mean the physically largest person or the oldest. Sentence 3, 'di-yi ci kan-dao-de yifu': the gloss gives 'floor' for di, but di-yi is the ordinal 'first'. I read the phrase as clothes never seen before, so new clothes. It could also mean clothes he himself sees for the first time. Sentences 7 and 13, 'tou bu hao', literally 'head not good': I read it as not clever or stupid. Taken literally it could mean a sick or hurt head. Sentence 7 does not say what such people cannot see. From sentence 6 I take it to be the clothes. In sentence 15 I read 'mei-you-de yifu' as clothes that do not exist. In sentence 19 the gloss splits nan-hai-zi into 'difficult-still-...', but as one word it means boy. In sentence 22 the gloss gives 'facing' for dui. Here it can only mean 'correct'. In sentence 23, 'hai zai zou' says he is still walking, carrying on. The text gives no reason why he keeps going.

notes: Translated by hand (2026-10-22) following the translate skill, whole dictionary. kb_memory returns this story's own book sentences (lesson none) at up to 100% shared, so step 2 hands over the reference text; 14 sentences adapt or keep one, each named in its source. Changed from them on purpose: tā-men hái shuō keeps the fools line the swindlers' claim; nán-hái-zi (boy) for nán-rén (man); méi-yǒu-de yīfu for the quoted "put on"; hái zài zǒu for qù-xià-qù (go-down-go). Grammar that will not parse as meant: (1) kàn-bù-dào reads first through verb-bu-verb's Either rule, which accepts two different verbs (see or not arrive); result-can-cant has no can't-with-object rule (only @verb de Res NP), so the book's "Tóu bù hǎo-de rén kàn-bù-dào zhè-zhǒng yīfu." can mean can't see only through Either: the object is dropped here. (2) shuō + a whole sentence has no rule, so the book's "rén-men jiù huì shuō wǒ tóu bù hǎo" cannot mean say I'm a fool; jué-dé used. (3) In "Rúguǒ tā shuō kàn-bù-dào, …" the first readings take tā shuō as his speech; the meant one is number 369, given as its full bracket. Length warnings left: sentences 3, 6, 7, 13 and 19 are 11 to 15 words. Glossary proposal: emperor -> zuì dà-de rén: the text's own literal note, and the dictionary's form of 皇帝 (yǐ-qián "Zhōngguó" zuì dà-de rén) ties every emperor to old China. Glossary proposal: swindler -> a sentence of its own, Tā-men duì rén shuō bù shì zhēn-de huà., then tā-men: the 10-word form never fits in a sentence. Glossary proposal: has no clothes on -> shēntǐ-shàng méi-yǒu yīfu: the form of wear is bǎ yīfu fàng zài shēntǐ-shàng. Glossary proposal: kept on doing -> hái zài + verb: keep on has no form. Glossary proposal: new (thing) -> dì-yī cì kàn-dào-de: xīn glosses as heart. Translated before kb_memory hid the stories' own lines (HAOSHUODE_MEMORY_SKIP), so some sentences reuse the book's lines and the book overlap is higher than a fresh run would give.
